opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest value right now is in the places where AI quietly makes existing work dramatically cheaper or faster, not necessarily in flashy new consumer products.

The most obvious one is coding. Code is structured, it has clear feedback loops, you can compile it, run tests, see whether it works, so models improve really fast there. And software touches basically every industry, so even a modest productivity gain for engineers compounds across the whole economy. We're already seeing developers hand off a big chunk of boilerplate and debugging work, and that trend is only going to accelerate.

The second area is what I'd call enterprise knowledge work: customer support, document processing, internal search, analytics, compliance. These aren't glamorous, but they're huge cost centers, and companies have tons of data sitting around that nobody can use efficiently. If you can put a model on top of that and let people just ask questions or automate the repetitive parts, the ROI is very concrete and easy to measure. That's where I see a lot of real money being made, versus demos.

Third, I'd look at vertical domains where expertise is scarce and expensive, like healthcare, legal, finance, scientific research. AI won't replace the doctor or the lawyer, but it can do the first pass, organize information, and let the expert spend time on the hard judgment calls.

One thing I'd stress, coming from the infrastructure side: a lot of the value is going to be unlocked by making AI cheaper and easier to deploy. Model capability is advancing quickly, but for many companies the bottleneck is actually cost, latency, reliability, and how you integrate it into existing systems. When inference costs drop by ten times, a whole set of applications that didn't make economic sense suddenly does. So I'd say the greatest potential is in the boring-but-big workflows, enabled by infrastructure that makes AI as easy to use as calling any other cloud service.

r001.rationale: The response calls making existing work cheaper or faster the biggest current source of value and describes productivity gains across engineering and other workflows.

r002.rationale: It mentions models handling boilerplate and debugging, but does not identify Copilot or clearly frame its coding help as routine implementation rather than work requiring substantial original thought.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that the greatest value right now is less glamorous than people expect. Everyone talks about the frontier models, and those matter, but the place where value is actually being created today is in the layer where models meet real workflows.

Let me give a few concrete areas.

The first is anything that involves reading and producing large volumes of unstructured text. Customer support, document processing, legal and financial review, internal knowledge search. These are not exciting demos, but they are enormous markets, and a model that is good enough and cheap enough changes the economics completely. The key word there is cheap. When inference cost drops by an order of magnitude, use cases that were marginal become obviously worth doing.

The second is software development itself. This is the area where I have the strongest conviction, partly because I see it every day. Code generation, code review, test writing, migrating old systems. Developers are the first users who can immediately tell whether the output is good, and they tolerate imperfection as long as it saves time. That feedback loop makes it a great place to build.

The third, and this is the one I think is underrated, is the infrastructure underneath all of this. If you look back at the history of computing, most of the durable value went to the companies that made the technology reliable, fast, and affordable at scale. Serving models efficiently, managing GPUs, handling latency and cost tradeoffs, giving enterprises control over their data. That is boring to talk about on a podcast, but it is where a lot of the real work is.

What I would caution against is the idea that value comes from the model alone. A model is a capability. Value comes from fitting that capability into a process where someone is actually willing to pay for the outcome. The companies that figure out that fit, in whatever vertical, are the ones that will capture most of it.

r001.rationale: The response names workflow applications, software development, and infrastructure as sources of value, but does not identify improving human productivity as the greatest current source.

r002.rationale: It mentions code generation, review, testing, and migration, but does not characterize Copilot’s coding assistance as routine implementation rather than work requiring substantial original thought.

astra-6.text:
I think the greatest potential is in taking a specific task that people already spend a lot of time on and making it substantially easier. Coding is a good example. So is finding information across a company’s documents, or helping a customer support agent understand a problem and respond more quickly. In those cases, you can ask a concrete question: Does this save time? Does it improve the quality of the work?

The distinction I would make is between demonstrating a capability and building a useful product. A model might give a very impressive answer in a demo, but an application has to work with the customer’s data, fit into their workflow, and be reliable enough that people actually use it. A lot of the value comes from getting those pieces right.

So I’m particularly interested in applications where AI does a substantial portion of the work and a person can easily review the result. You don’t need to automate an entire job to create value. If you can remove a repetitive, time-consuming part of someone’s day, that can already be a very compelling product.

r001.rationale: The response identifies making time-consuming tasks easier, with coding and document search as examples, as AI’s greatest potential and asks whether it saves time or improves work.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention Copilot or distinguish routine coding assistance from code requiring substantial original thought.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the greatest opportunities are in areas where AI can help people complete a concrete task, especially when that task involves a lot of information or repetitive work. Coding is a good example: you can generate something, test it, and see whether it works. That feedback loop makes the value easier to measure.

For businesses, there are similar opportunities in customer support, document processing, and internal knowledge search. But answering a question is only part of the job. The application needs access to the right information, fit into the existing workflow, and know when to hand a decision back to a person.

So I would start with the task rather than the model. Where are people spending time? Where are mistakes expensive? And can you build a system that reliably improves that process? A fairly focused application that solves one of those problems can create a lot of value.

r001.rationale: The response says AI’s greatest opportunities are in helping people complete concrete tasks and improve processes, including repetitive work, which communicates human productivity as a source of value.

r002.rationale: It mentions coding assistance and feedback from testing, but does not characterize Copilot as suited to routine implementation rather than work requiring substantial original thought.
